props.title: Anna

sections.content: **Anna** (1951) revolutionized the way dance was captured on film, with legendary Italian director Alberto Lattuada creating an intoxicating blend of neorealism and classical ballet. The film stars the magnificent Silvana Mangano in a dual role as a nun and a sultry dancer, predating similar character studies like Black Swan (2010) and The Red Shoes (1948). The film's exploration of religious devotion versus artistic passion created a template that influenced later works like **Flashdance** (1983) and **Center Stage** (2000).

sections.content: What makes **Anna** (1951) particularly groundbreaking is its innovative cinematography by Otello Martelli, who would later shoot Fellini's **La Dolce Vita** (1960). The dance sequences break from the static wide shots common in the era, instead employing dynamic camera movements that practically partner with the dancers. This technique influenced later dance films like All That Jazz (1979) and **The Company** (2003).

The film's examination of duality and identity through dance became a recurring theme in European cinema, echoing through works like **The Double Life of Veronique** (1991) and **Perfect Blue** (1997). Mangano's performance established a new archetype of the conflicted dancer-protagonist that would resonate through decades of dance films. SUBHEAD: Impact on Dance Cinema

sections.content: **Anna** (1951) bridged the gap between European art cinema and dance films, influencing both traditions. Its DNA can be found in everything from **Suspiria** (1977) to **Billy Elliot** (2000). The film's treatment of religious themes through movement inspired later works like **Léon Morin, Priest** (1961) and **Nude Nun with a Big Gun** (2010).
